author: vedran-obucina
description: In the 2nd century, Lucian of Samosata was already sending his narrator to the Moon. But it took the Scientific Revolution, and then Mary Shelley's monster, to turn those dreams into a new way of questioning change.

hero.hook: A trip to the Moon in the 2nd century, a monster stitched together in 1818, a name found in 1929: science fiction is far older than its rockets.

blocks.text: Science fiction does not begin with spaceships. For centuries, people imagined journeys to the Moon, strange societies and artificially made beings. In the **2nd century**, the Greek author [[Lucian of Samosata]] wrote his *True Story*: its narrator travels to the Moon and meets surprising creatures there.

It is not yet science fiction in the modern sense. Lucian exaggerates, mocks, and wields satire to laugh at human ideas. But his tale already asks the essential question: what would the world look like if reality worked differently? Something changed the day people began to believe that science could explain nature and reshape the future.

The [[Scientific Revolution]] is the period when observation, measurement and experiment overturned European ideas about nature. In the **17th century**, people looked at the Moon and the planets with fresh interest. The telescope, which Galileo turned toward the sky in 1610, showed that the heavens were neither perfect nor unchanging, contrary to what many had believed.

blocks.caption: Galileo's drawings of the Moon, published in 1610: craters and ridges along the line of shadow.

blocks.text: The astronomer [[Johannes Kepler]] seized on this new knowledge in his *Somnium*, "The Dream," published in **1634**, after his death. In it he imagines a journey to the Moon and describes what the Earth would look like from space. The text has no clear literary genre. But scientific ideas are no longer mere backdrop: they become the material from which a writer builds an imaginary world.

In **1818**, [[Mary Shelley]] published *Frankenstein*. It is a monster story, but its central question is new: what happens when a scientist uses knowledge to create life? Victor Frankenstein crosses a line that people regard as unnatural. When his creature comes alive, scientific success brings him fame, but also disaster.

blocks.caption: The creature awakens on the laboratory table: frontispiece of the 1831 edition.

blocks.text: Shelley writes about responsibility, fear and suffering. She asks whether human ambition moves faster than our ability to understand its consequences. It is the very question of the [[Industrial Revolution]]: machines, factories and new technologies were changing life at full speed. Technology stops being an abstract idea when it enters cities, workshops and even bodies. Science fiction gains its full force when technology becomes the source of the great problems.

sections.title: Frankenstein gives the genre its shape

blocks.text: Science fiction stories existed long before the term itself. Jules Verne and H. G. Wells developed great ideas: space travel, extraordinary machines, time travel, societies of the future. In the **1920s**, the American editor [[Hugo Gernsback]] helped these stories find their place. His magazines published tales of science, technology, inventions and possible futures.

blocks.caption: The cover of the first issue of Amazing Stories, April 1926, illustrated by Frank R. Paul.

blocks.text: Readers could now follow a whole genre, not just a few scattered books. Gernsback did not "create" science fiction. He gave it a recognized name, a public and commercial space, a familiarity. The term "science fiction" took hold at the end of the decade, when he attached it to his magazine *Science Wonder Stories*. The genre finally had a literary address.

Hugo Gernsback first spoke of "scientifiction" before "science fiction" became established. He launched *Amazing Stories* in 1926, then helped popularize the modern name with *Science Wonder Stories* in 1929.

sections.title: A name that came much later

blocks.text: Spaceships, robots, aliens, scientists: none of that is what defines science fiction first. Its deepest subject is change. What happens when a discovery, a technology or a scientific idea transforms human life? The same genre can travel to distant planets, explore artificial intelligence, play with genetic engineering or describe societies that do not yet exist.

The imagined world has to be strange, new, spectacular. But at bottom it asks questions about our own world, its fears, its anxieties and its hopes. Frightening novel or thriller on screen, science fiction dives into human ethics and psychology. It exists whenever an imagined future is used to question the present.

Science fiction is born when science becomes raw material for stories, from Kepler to Mary Shelley, and it lives on whenever an imagined future is used to ask the questions the present cannot yet answer.
